nodes.name: Resurgence large-order relation with Stokes constants
nodes.section: 1 Introduction
nodes.statement: \be \Phi^{(0)}_{k \gg 1} \quad \longleftrightarrow \quad \boldsymbol{S_1} \left[ \Phi^{(1)}_\ell \right] + \boldsymbol{S_2} \left[ \Phi^{(2)}_\ell \right] + \boldsymbol{S_3} \left[ \Phi^{(3)}_\ell \right] + \cdots. \ee
nodes.statement_short: Schematic resurgence relation: the large-order growth of the perturbative coefficients is controlled by all multi-instanton sectors weighted by Stokes constants $S_n$.

nodes.name: Computation of the Stokes constants
nodes.section: 1 Introduction
nodes.statement: So how do we compute them? This is generically a hard problem, specially for nonlinear systems, and one which we shall discuss at length in this paper. The origin of these Stokes constants predates resurgence by over one hundred years: they of course arise with the discovery of Stokes phenomena \cite{s64} (see, \textit{e.g.}, the excellent review \cite{b91} in a closely related context). When the transseries is first assembled, all its nonperturbative content $\Phi^{(n)}$ is exponentially suppressed; in fact the higher the instanton number the greater the exponential damping. This means that already the one-instanton contribution is invisible from the point-of-view of the perturbative power series---at least as long as the (overall) argument of the exponential is negative. But as one changes the couplings or other parameters in the theory along the complex plane, this argument may vary and consequentially these exponentially suppressed contributions may change dominance. In fact they can become of the same order as the perturbative series and, eventually, even exponentially \textit{enhanced} as compared to $\Phi^{(0)}$. This is the essence of Stokes phenomena: small, suppressed exponentials, hidden behind perturbation theory, may actually grow to become the dominant contribution. The transseries formalism already incorporates Stokes phenomena in the sense that it assembles all non-analytic exponential contributions together. The Stokes constants then precisely control how the transseries changes as one varies the couplings across their complex domains and different types of Stokes phenomena may occur. As we shall show later, this is accomplished by having the \textit{transseries parameters} $\boldsymbol{\sigma}$ transform at the Stokes lines, with these transformations explicitly dependent upon the Stokes constants ``attached'' to the corresponding Stokes line (in the simplest cases these are just shifts $\boldsymbol{\sigma} \to \boldsymbol{\sigma} + \boldsymbol{S_1}$, such that if one starts off with the perturbative series alone, $\boldsymbol{\sigma}=\boldsymbol{0}$, upon crossing a Stokes line the exponential contributions become ``turned on'' with their weight measured by $\boldsymbol{S_1}$). How general transseries incorporate Stokes phenomena was recently discussed in \cite{as13}. The fundamental role played by the Stokes constants in the nonperturbative construction of a given observable should be now clear. They allow for precise, quantitative statements concerning the large-order resurgent behaviour of its different sectors; and they precisely quantify Stokes phenomena, allowing for a fully nonperturbative exploration of the whole parameter (coupling) space. Yet, computing them may be very hard. For instance, in the examples of the Painlev\'e~I \cite{msw07, gikm10, asv11} or the Painlev\'e~II \cite{m08, sv13} equations, out of a possibly infinite set of Stokes constants only one (in each problem) was accessible to analytic calculation. All others had to be determined numerically. Even worse, most of these resulting numbers seemed to be transcendental. Having a first principles guide to the computation of Stokes constants is thus a critical step towards achieving analytical control over this type of nonperturbative constructions.
nodes.statement_short: Determine the Stokes constants $S_n$ that quantify resurgence relations and Stokes phenomena; generically hard, especially for nonlinear systems.

nodes.name: Resonance from $\BZ$-linearly dependent instanton actions
nodes.section: 1 Introduction
nodes.statement: There is one more feature which may be found in general resurgent asymptotics and we still wish to mention: \textit{resonance}. While we have been talking about a single instanton action, in many scenarios one may in fact have \textit{several} instanton (or renormalon) actions. The number of nonperturbative sectors then multiplies accordingly. For simplicity, let us assume there are only two instanton actions, $A_1$ and $A_2$, and the nonperturbative sectors are organized as $(n,m)$ corresponding to an exponential factor of the form $\sim n A_1 + m A_2$. The reader immediately realizes that a door is now open towards new phenomena: indeed, if the two actions happen to be $\BZ$-linearly dependent, then there is $n^\star$, $m^\star$ such that $n^\star A_1 + m^\star A_2 = 0$ and the nonperturbative exponential contributions ``collapse'' to order one, no longer suppressed or enhanced. Such phenomena have appeared recurrently in recent string theoretic examples \cite{gikm10, asv11, sv13}. In these cases both the large-order resurgence relations as well as the transseries structure will change, in order to incorporate new (nonperturbative) resonant sectors, and logarithms may appear throughout. Because general physical problems may depend upon many parameters, it is conceivable that resonance is ``tunable'' and may generically appear in many examples. We shall later discuss in a very explicit example how this may come about and what are its implications.
nodes.statement_short: When two instanton actions are $\BZ$-linearly dependent the nonperturbative exponentials collapse to order one, changing both transseries structure and large-order relations.

nodes.name: Borel transform
nodes.section: 2 Resurgent Analysis of a Quartic-Potential Integral
nodes.statement: \begin{align} \CB \colon \BC [[x]] &\rightarrow \BC [[s]] \\ x^{\alpha+1} &\mapsto \CB \left[ x^{\alpha+1} \right](s) = \frac{s^{\alpha}}{\Gamma(\alpha+1)}. \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: The Borel transform sends $x^{\alpha+1}\mapsto s^{\alpha}/\Gamma(\alpha+1)$, trading factorial growth for a finite radius of convergence.
nodes.genus: a linear map acting on formal power series

nodes.name: Convergence and analytic continuation of the Borel transform
nodes.section: 2 Resurgent Analysis of a Quartic-Potential Integral
nodes.statement: This produces a new series, $\CB [\Phi^{(0)}] (s)$, out of the asymptotic series \eqref{divergent}, which has finite \textit{non-zero} convergence radius, as its coefficients no longer grow factorially but instead only exponentially fast. It may thus be analytically continued throughout $s \in \BC$, into a \textit{function}, albeit having singularities and branch cuts.
nodes.statement_short: The Borel transform of an asymptotic series converges near the origin and continues to a function with singularities and branch cuts.
assumptions: out of the asymptotic series \eqref{divergent}
conclusions: It may thus be analytically continued throughout $s \in \BC$, into a \textit{function}, albeit having singularities and branch cuts.

nodes.name: Borel resummation
nodes.section: 2 Resurgent Analysis of a Quartic-Potential Integral
nodes.statement: the \textit{Borel resummation} (or inverse Borel transform) \be \CS_\theta \Phi^{(0)} (x) = \int_0^{\rme^{\rmi\theta}\infty} \rmd s\, \CB[\Phi^{(0)}](s)\, \rme^{-\frac{s}{x}} \ee \noindent finally associates a finite value to the divergent sum \eqref{divergent}, for each $x$.
nodes.statement_short: A Laplace-type integral of the Borel transform along a non-singular direction $\theta$ assigning a finite value to the divergent series.

nodes.name: Stokes line
nodes.section: 2 Resurgent Analysis of a Quartic-Potential Integral
nodes.statement: Indeed, if $\CB [\Phi^{(0)}] (s)$ has singularities along $\theta$, this (singular) direction is now known as a \textit{Stokes line}, where \eqref{borelresum} is no longer well-defined: there is an \textit{ambiguity} concerning along which direction should these singularities be avoided by the integration contour.
nodes.statement_short: A direction on the Borel plane along which the Borel transform is singular, so that Borel resummation becomes ambiguous.

nodes.name: Lateral Borel resummations
nodes.section: 2 Resurgent Analysis of a Quartic-Potential Integral
nodes.statement: In order to solve this issue, one first defines \textit{lateral} Borel resummations, $\CS_{\theta^{\pm}} \Phi^{(0)} (x)$, which avoid all singularities via a contour just to the left (to the right) of the direction $\theta$.
nodes.statement_short: Resummations $\CS_{\theta^{\pm}}$ whose contours pass just to the left or right of the Borel singularities along $\theta$.

nodes.name: Stokes automorphism
nodes.section: 2 Resurgent Analysis of a Quartic-Potential Integral
nodes.statement: The lateral Borel resummations lead to \textit{distinct} sectorial resummations of our original asymptotic series, but they are nonetheless \textit{connected} via the so-called \textit{Stokes automorphism} $\underline{\mathfrak{S}}_\theta$, \be \CS_{\theta^+} = \CS_{\theta^-} \circ \underline{\mathfrak{S}}_\theta. \ee
nodes.statement_short: The operator $\underline{\mathfrak{S}}_\theta$ connecting the two lateral Borel resummations across a Stokes line.

nodes.name: Alien derivative
nodes.section: 2 Resurgent Analysis of a Quartic-Potential Integral
nodes.statement: This is also the point where \textit{alien calculus} kicks in, as the Stokes automorphism may be computed in terms of the \textit{alien derivative}, $\Delta_\omega$, a differential operator encoding the singular behaviour of the Borel transform at the point $\omega$.
nodes.statement_short: $\Delta_\omega$ is a differential operator recording the singular behaviour of the Borel transform at $\omega$.
differentia: encoding the singular behaviour of the Borel transform at the point $\omega$

nodes.name: One-parameter transseries
nodes.section: 2 Resurgent Analysis of a Quartic-Potential Integral
nodes.statement: For example, a transseries \textit{ansatz} for our resurgent function, depending on a single parameter $\sigma$, could be \be \Phi (x,\sigma) = \sum_{n=0}^{+\infty} \sigma^n\, \Phi^{(n)} (x), \ee
nodes.statement_short: A formal sum $\Phi(x,\sigma)=\sum_n \sigma^n \Phi^{(n)}(x)$ over all instanton sectors, weighted by the transseries parameter $\sigma$.

nodes.name: $n$-instanton sector of a transseries
nodes.section: 2 Resurgent Analysis of a Quartic-Potential Integral
nodes.statement: \be \Phi^{(n)} (x) \simeq \rme^{-n \frac{A}{x}}\, \sum_{g=1}^{+\infty} \Phi_g^{(n)}\, x^{g + \beta_n}, \ee \noindent with $A$ the instanton action and $\beta_n$ a characteristic exponent.
nodes.statement_short: Each instanton sector is a non-analytic exponential $\rme^{-nA/x}$ times an asymptotic power series.

nodes.name: Stokes phenomenon as a shift of the transseries parameter
nodes.section: 2 Resurgent Analysis of a Quartic-Potential Integral
nodes.statement: applying the Stokes automorphism \eqref{stokesauto} one finds \be \CS_{+} \Phi (x,\sigma) = \CS_{-} \Phi \left( x, \sigma + S_1 \right), \ee \noindent where $S_1$ is a Stokes constant as in \eqref{resurgence_stokes}.
nodes.statement_short: Crossing a Stokes line shifts the transseries parameter by the Stokes constant, $\sigma \to \sigma + S_1$.

nodes.name: Quartic partition function
nodes.section: 2.1 Phase Diagram from Stokes Phenomena
nodes.statement: Consider the ``quartic partition function'', described by \be Z (\hbar) = \frac{1}{2\pi} \int_{\Gamma} \rmd z\, \rme^{- \frac{1}{\hbar} V(z)}, \ee \noindent where $V(z)$ is the quartic potential \be V(z) = \frac{1}{2} z^2 - \frac{\lambda}{24} z^4, \ee \noindent with coupling constant $\lambda$, and $\Gamma$ is a contour to be specified.
nodes.statement_short: A one-dimensional contour integral $Z(\hbar)=\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_\Gamma \rmd z\, \rme^{-V(z)/\hbar}$ with quartic potential.

nodes.name: Quartic potential
nodes.section: 2.1 Phase Diagram from Stokes Phenomena
nodes.statement: \be V(z) = \frac{1}{2} z^2 - \frac{\lambda}{24} z^4, \ee \noindent with coupling constant $\lambda$

nodes.name: Quartic partition function in the variable $x = \lambda\hbar$
nodes.section: 2.1 Phase Diagram from Stokes Phenomena
nodes.statement: With a simple change of variables the partition function \eqref{quarticintegral} may be written as \be Z (x) = \frac{\sqrt{\hbar}}{2\pi} \int_{\Gamma} \rmd z\, \exp \left( - \frac{1}{2} z^2 + \frac{x}{24} z^4 \right), \ee \noindent which explicitly illustrates how all non-trivial dependence occurs through the variable $x \equiv \lambda \hbar$, and this is what we shall study in the following.

nodes.name: Path of steepest descent
nodes.section: 2.1 Phase Diagram from Stokes Phenomena
nodes.statement: one deforms the contour of integration into the infinite, oriented path of steepest descent through $z^*$, defined as \be \im \left( V(z) - V(z^*) \right) = 0, \ee \noindent and increasing away from $z^*$.

nodes.name: Stokes lines of the quartic partition function
nodes.section: 2.1 Phase Diagram from Stokes Phenomena
nodes.statement: This will occur when \be \im \left( V(z^*_{\pm}) - V(z^*_0) \right) = 0 \quad \Leftrightarrow \quad \im\ \frac{1}{x} = 0, \ee \noindent corresponding to $\arg x = 0, \pi$ (these lines are very distinctive in figure~\ref{steepest}). These are\footnote{Note that the definitions of Stokes and anti-Stokes lines are usually reversed between the mathematical and physical literatures. In this work we are using the appropriate definitions within the resurgence framework. As such, the reader who has been exposed to these ideas before should pay attention to our precise definitions.} the \textit{Stokes lines} for the quartic partition-function, where, because other (suppressed) saddles start contributing to the evaluation of the integral, subleading exponentials likewise start contributing to the asymptotics.
nodes.statement_short: The Stokes lines $\arg x = 0,\pi$ are where the steepest-descent contour meets a second saddle and subleading exponentials switch on.

nodes.name: Anti-Stokes line
nodes.section: 2.1 Phase Diagram from Stokes Phenomena
nodes.statement: when they becomes of the same magnitude as the leading term, we reach what is known as an \textit{anti-Stokes line}. Different exponential contributions are of the same magnitude when both saddles have the same real part, \be \re \left( V(z^*_{\pm}) - V(z^*_0) \right) = 0 \quad \Leftrightarrow \quad \re\ \frac{1}{x} = 0, \ee \noindent corresponding to $\arg x = \frac{\pi}{2}, \frac{3\pi}{2}$
nodes.statement_short: The directions where different exponential contributions have equal magnitude, here $\re(1/x)=0$.

nodes.name: Stokes phenomenon
nodes.section: 2.1 Phase Diagram from Stokes Phenomena
nodes.statement: What we have just described is the Stokes phenomenon: in an asymptotic approximation, \textit{different} asymptotic formulae hold, on different sectors, for the \textit{same} analytic function. As we shall see, transseries precisely capture all these possible asymptotic formulae in a single go.
nodes.statement_short: Different asymptotic formulae hold on different sectors for the same analytic function; transseries package them all together.

nodes.name: Lee--Yang interpretation of Stokes phenomena as phase transitions
nodes.section: 2.1 Phase Diagram from Stokes Phenomena
nodes.statement: In the meantime, it is also interesting to understand the physical interpretation where Stokes phenomenon describes phase transitions \cite{ps93}, building upon the Lee--Yang construction \cite{ly52a, ly52b} (see \cite{gg07} as well). In the Lee--Yang set-up, the finite-size grand-canonical partition function is first written as a polynomial. A phase transition then arises if, in the thermodynamic limit, the zeros of this polynomial condense onto lines describing phase boundaries. In the case of the quartic partition function (where the asymptotic approximation plays the role of the thermodynamic limit), it is simple to see that phase transitions occur at the anti-Stokes lines, from the ``one-saddle'' phase to the ``two-saddle'' phase and back again.
nodes.statement_short: Anti-Stokes lines are phase boundaries in a Lee--Yang sense, with partition-function zeros condensing on the imaginary axis.

nodes.name: Linear ODE for the quartic partition function
nodes.section: 2.2 Basic Formulae for Resurgent Analysis
nodes.statement: This is most simply done by first noticing that this integral satisfies a second-order \textit{linear} ordinary differential equation\footnote{As mentioned, peeling off an exponential piece and changing variables, this is the modified Bessel equation.} (ODE), \be 16 x^2\, Z'' (x) + \left( 32 x - 24 \right) Z' (x) + 3\, Z (x) = 0. \ee
nodes.statement_short: The quartic partition function obeys a second-order linear ODE (the modified Bessel equation in disguise).

nodes.name: Instanton actions of the quartic partition function
nodes.section: 2.2 Basic Formulae for Resurgent Analysis
nodes.statement: The quadratic equation for $A$ yields the two solutions \be A = 0 \qquad \text{or} \qquad A = \frac{3}{2} \ee \noindent as expected from our earlier saddle-point analysis

nodes.name: Asymptotic series of the quartic partition function
nodes.section: 2.2 Basic Formulae for Resurgent Analysis
nodes.statement_short: Closed-form coefficients for the perturbative and one-instanton sectors, growing as $A^{-n} n!$.

nodes.name: Residual coefficients
nodes.section: 2.2 Basic Formulae for Resurgent Analysis
nodes.statement: Notice that one still has to evaluate the \textit{constant} ($x$-independent) contributions, $Z^{(0)}_0$ and $Z^{(1)}_0$, sometimes denoted by \textit{residual coefficients} in the resurgence literature.

nodes.name: Asymptotic evaluation of the quartic partition function
nodes.section: 2.2 Basic Formulae for Resurgent Analysis
nodes.statement: The asymptotic evaluation of the quartic partition function thus boils down to \bea Z^{(0)} (x) &\simeq& \sqrt{\frac{\hbar}{2\pi}}\, \sum_{n=0}^{+\infty} \left( \frac{2}{3} \right)^n \frac{(4n)!}{2^{6n}\, (2n)!\, n!}\, x^n, \\ Z^{(1)} (x) &\simeq& -\frac{\rmi}{\sqrt{2}}\, \sqrt{\frac{\hbar}{2\pi}}\, \rme^{-\frac{3}{2x}}\, \sum_{n=0}^{+\infty} (-1)^n \left( \frac{2}{3} \right)^n \frac{(4n)!}{2^{6n}\, (2n)!\, n!}\, x^n. \eea

nodes.name: Transseries solution of the quartic partition function
nodes.section: 2.2 Basic Formulae for Resurgent Analysis
nodes.statement: One finds: \be \CZ (x, \sigma_{0}, \sigma_{1}) = \sigma_{0}\, Z^{(0)}(x) + \sigma_{1}\, Z^{(1)}(x). \ee \noindent This is in fact the \textit{transseries solution} to the problem, in the sense that it incorporates all saddles. The transseries parameters are $\sigma_{0}$ and $\sigma_{1}$, and it is also clear how they are parameterizing boundary conditions or contours of integration, depending upon the point-of-view.
nodes.statement_short: The general solution of the linear ODE is the two-term transseries $\sigma_0 Z^{(0)} + \sigma_1 Z^{(1)}$, with $\sigma_i$ fixing boundary conditions.

nodes.name: Borel transforms of the quartic sectors
nodes.section: 2.2 Basic Formulae for Resurgent Analysis
nodes.statement: It is straightforward to obtain\footnote{Note that the Borel transform \eqref{boreltrans} is undefined for the residual coefficient, with $\alpha+1=0$. This is simply handled by dropping this coefficient and only adding it back-in at the end---its contribution is trivial to include at any stage. Our Borel transforms thus follow from \eqref{coeff-quartic} and \eqref{coeff-quartic-inst} with the asymptotic series starting at $n=1$. } \bea \CB [\Phi_{0}] (s) &=& \frac{1}{8}\, \sqrt{\frac{\hbar}{2\pi}}\, {}_2 F_{1} \left( \frac{5}{4}, \frac{7}{4}, 2 \right. \left| \frac{2s}{3} \right), \\ \CB [\Phi_{1}] (s) &=& \frac{\rmi}{8 \sqrt{2}}\, \sqrt{\frac{\hbar}{2\pi}}\, {}_2 F_{1} \left( \frac{5}{4}, \frac{7}{4}, 2 \right. \left| - \frac{2s}{3} \right), \eea
nodes.statement_short: Both Borel transforms are hypergeometric ${}_2F_1$ functions with singularities at $s=\pm A$.

nodes.name: Borel singularity expansions exhibiting resurgence
nodes.section: 2.2 Basic Formulae for Resurgent Analysis
nodes.statement: \bea \CB [\Phi_{0}] (s) &=& \left( + 2 \right) \times \frac{Z_{0}^{(1)}}{2\pi\rmi \left( s-A \right)} + \left( + 2 \right) \times \CB [\Phi_{1}] \left( s-A \right) \frac{\log \left( s-A \right)}{2\pi\rmi} + \text{holomorphic}, \\ \CB [\Phi_{1}] (s) &=& \left( - 1 \right) \times \frac{Z_{0}^{(0)}}{2\pi\rmi \left( s+A \right)} + \left( - 1 \right) \times \CB [\Phi_{0}] \left( s+A \right) \frac{\log \left( s+A \right)}{2\pi\rmi} + \text{holomorphic}. \eea
nodes.statement_short: At its Borel singularity each sector reproduces the other sector -- the origin of the name resurgence.

nodes.name: Alien derivative in the linear case
nodes.section: 2.2 Basic Formulae for Resurgent Analysis
nodes.statement: a definition for such an operator naturally follows from the previous two equations, as\footnote{It is very important to keep in mind that this definition \textit{only holds} in the present \textit{linear} case. It will \textit{not} hold for \textit{nonlinear} problems, where it will require (substantial) modification. More on this in the following.} \be \Delta_\omega := \rme^{\frac{\omega}{x}} \left( \CS_{\theta^+} - \CS_{\theta^-} \right), \ee \noindent if the na\"\i ve action of $\Delta_\omega$ results in a ``pure'' power-series (\textit{i.e.}, another transseries block, without any exponential factors), and $\Delta_\omega := 0$ otherwise
nodes.statement_short: For linear problems $\Delta_\omega := \rme^{\omega/x}(\CS_{\theta^+}-\CS_{\theta^-})$ when the result is a pure power series, and zero otherwise.

nodes.name: Resurgence relations for the quartic partition function
nodes.section: 2.2 Basic Formulae for Resurgent Analysis
nodes.statement: \bea \Delta_{+A} \Phi_{0} &=& \left( - 2 \right) \times \Phi_{1}, \\ \Delta_{-A} \Phi_{1} &=& \Phi_{0}. \eea \noindent Our departure equations may here be recovered by reading these expressions as follows: the Borel transform of $\Phi_{0}$ has a singularity at $\omega=+A$ which is given by the \textit{Stokes coefficient} $S_1 = -2$, multiplied by the Borel transform of $\Phi_{1}$
nodes.statement_short: The two-node alien chain of the quartic partition function, with Stokes coefficients $S_1=-2$ and $S_{-1}=1$.

nodes.name: Stokes automorphism as the exponential of alien derivatives
nodes.section: 2.2 Basic Formulae for Resurgent Analysis
nodes.statement: is essentially given by the exponential of the alien derivative (why this is so will hopefully be motivated by the end result that follows), \be \underline{\mathfrak{S}}_\theta = \exp \left( \sum_{\left\{ \omega_\theta \right\}} \rme^{-\frac{\omega_\theta}{x}} \Delta_{\omega_\theta} \right). \ee \noindent Herein, the set $\left\{ \omega_\theta \right\}$ corresponds to all possible Borel singularities along the direction
nodes.statement_short: $\underline{\mathfrak{S}}_\theta$ exponentiates the sum of alien derivatives at all Borel singularities along $\theta$.

nodes.name: Monodromy of the quartic transseries
nodes.section: 2.2 Basic Formulae for Resurgent Analysis
nodes.statement: while if we move four times around the origin we recover the identity, \be \left( \underline{\mathfrak{S}}_\pi \underline{\mathfrak{S}}_0 \right)^4 = \boldsymbol{1}. \ee \noindent This expression tells us what is the monodromy encoded in the transseries solution to the quartic integral, which is thus best understood as a multi-sheeted Riemann surface
nodes.statement_short: Four turns around the origin return the transseries to itself: the solution lives on a four-sheeted Riemann surface.
assumptions: if we move four times around the origin

nodes.name: Stokes matrix at $\theta=0$ for the quartic thimbles
nodes.section: 2.2 Basic Formulae for Resurgent Analysis
nodes.statement: These conditions may be compactly expressed as \begin{equation} \left( \begin{array}{ccc} \CJ_0 \\ \CJ_+ \\ \CJ_- \end{array} \right) \to S_{\circlearrowleft}^{(0)} \left( \begin{array}{ccc} \CJ_0 \\ \CJ_+ \\ \CJ_- \end{array} \right) = \left( \begin{array}{ccc} 1 & -1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{array} \right) \left( \begin{array}{ccc} \CJ_0 \\ \CJ_+ \\ \CJ_- \end{array} \right), \end{equation} \noindent where $S_{\circlearrowleft}^{(0)}$ is the ``Stokes matrix'' associated to $\theta=0$.

nodes.name: Monodromy matrix of the steepest-descent contours
nodes.section: 2.2 Basic Formulae for Resurgent Analysis
nodes.statement: If we finally define the \textit{monodromy matrix} $\mathfrak{M} := S_{\circlearrowleft}^{(\pi)} \cdot S_{\circlearrowleft}^{(0)}$ it is simple to check that $\mathfrak{M}^4 = \boldsymbol{1}$, which is the steepest-descent equivalent of the monodromy relation \eqref{quarticmonodromy}.
assumptions: the \textit{monodromy matrix} $\mathfrak{M} := S_{\circlearrowleft}^{(\pi)} \cdot S_{\circlearrowleft}^{(0)}$

nodes.name: Stokes discontinuity
nodes.section: 2.3 Asymptotics and Large-Order Behaviour: Partition Function
nodes.statement: This implies that there is a \textit{discontinuity} of the asymptotic expansions\footnote{So that the nature of this discontinuity is completely clear, let us repeat what we wrote earlier concerning Stokes phenomenon: in an asymptotic approximation, \textit{different} asymptotic formulae hold, on different sectors, for the \textit{same} analytic function. In this way, it is this discontinuity which then relates them to each other.}, $\disc_\theta$, which must relate to the Stokes automorphism as \be \disc_\theta = \1 - \underline{\mathfrak{S}}_\theta, \ee \noindent so that $\CS_{\theta^+} - \CS_{\theta^-} = - \CS_{\theta^-} \circ \disc_\theta$
nodes.statement_short: $\disc_\theta = \1 - \underline{\mathfrak{S}}_\theta$ measures the jump of the asymptotic expansions across a Stokes line.

nodes.name: Cauchy's theorem for a function with a discontinuity
nodes.section: 2.3 Asymptotics and Large-Order Behaviour: Partition Function
nodes.statement: Now given a function $F(x)$, with a discontinuity along some ray starting from the origin on the complex plane along the direction $\theta$, Cauchy's theorem translates to \be F(x) = - \frac{1}{2\pi\rmi} \int_{0}^{\rme^{\rmi\theta} \infty} \rmd w\, \frac{\disc_\theta F(w)}{w-x}, \ee

nodes.name: Large-order relation for the quartic partition function
nodes.section: 2.3 Asymptotics and Large-Order Behaviour: Partition Function
nodes.statement: One may regard this expression as a large-order relation (see figure~\ref{fig:quarticpartfunc-largeorder}), \be Z^{(0)}_n \simeq -\frac{2}{2\pi\rmi}\, \frac{\left(n-1\right)!}{A^n} \left( Z^{(1)}_0 + \frac{Z^{(1)}_1 A}{n-1} + \frac{Z^{(1)}_2 A^2}{\left( n-1 \right) \left( n-2 \right)} + \cdots \right); \ee
nodes.statement_short: The perturbative coefficients grow as $(n-1)!/A^n$ with $1/n$ corrections given by the one-instanton coefficients.

nodes.name: Nonlinear ODE for the quartic free energy
nodes.section: 2.4 First Steps Towards Nonlinear Resurgent Analysis
nodes.statement: this time around the quartic-potential free energy satisfies a \textit{nonlinear} second-order ODE, \be 16 x^2\, F'' (x) + 16 x^2 \left( F'(x) \right)^2 + \left( 32 x - 24 \right) F' (x) + 3 = 0. \ee
nodes.statement_short: The quartic free energy $F=\log Z$ obeys a nonlinear second-order ODE, forcing an infinite tower of multi-instanton sectors.

nodes.name: Recursion for the perturbative free-energy coefficients
nodes.section: 2.4 First Steps Towards Nonlinear Resurgent Analysis
nodes.statement: An asymptotic perturbative solution $F (x) \simeq \sum_{n=0}^{+\infty} F_n^{(0)} x^n$ yields the recursion (determining it) \be F_{n+1}^{(0)} = \frac{2}{3} \left( n\, F_n^{(0)} + \frac{1}{n+1} \sum_{k=1}^{n-1} k \left(n-k\right) F_k^{(0)}\, F_{n-k}^{(0)} \right), \ee \noindent with $F_1^{(0)} = \frac{1}{8}$ and $F_0^{(0)}$ an integration constant.

nodes.name: One-parameter transseries for the quartic free energy
nodes.section: 2.4 First Steps Towards Nonlinear Resurgent Analysis
nodes.statement: the following one-parameter transseries \be F (x, \sigma) = \sum_{\ell=0}^{+\infty} \sigma^\ell\, \rme^{-\frac{\ell A}{x}}\, \Phi_{\ell} (x). \ee \noindent Here $\sigma$ is the transseries instanton-counting parameter (an integration constant parameterizing boundary conditions), and the $\Phi_{\ell} (x)$ are the transseries building blocks, \textit{i.e.}, the asymptotic expansions associated to each (multi) instanton sector, \be \Phi_{\ell} (x) \simeq \sum_{n=0}^{+\infty} F_n^{(\ell)}\, x^n. \ee
nodes.statement_short: An infinite tower of multi-instanton sectors $\Phi_\ell$ weighted by $\sigma^\ell \rme^{-\ell A/x}$.

nodes.name: Borel singularity structure of a one-parameter transseries
nodes.section: 2.4 First Steps Towards Nonlinear Resurgent Analysis
nodes.statement: \be \CB [\Phi_n] (s) \Big|_{s=kA} = \mathsf{S}_{n\to n+k} \times \CB [\Phi_{n+k}] \left( s-kA\right)\, \frac{\log \left( s-kA \right)}{2\pi\rmi}, \qquad k\neq0. \ee \noindent Near the singularity $s=kA$ of $\CB [\Phi_n] (s)$ one finds the \textit{resurgence} of the $\Phi_{n+k}$ sector, through its corresponding Borel transform
nodes.statement_short: Near $s=kA$ the Borel transform of $\Phi_n$ reproduces $\Phi_{n+k}$ with a logarithmic branch cut.

nodes.name: Borel residue
nodes.section: 2.4 First Steps Towards Nonlinear Resurgent Analysis
nodes.statement: One also finds a proportionality constant $\mathsf{S}_{n\to n+k}$, the \textit{``Borel residue''}, numerically characterizing each distinct logarithmic singularity.

nodes.name: Resurgence relations for a one-parameter transseries
nodes.section: 2.4 First Steps Towards Nonlinear Resurgent Analysis
nodes.statement: \be \Delta_{k A} \Phi_n = S_{k} \left(n+k\right) \Phi_{n+k}, \qquad k \le 1 \text{ and } k \neq 0. \ee \noindent These \textit{resurgence relations} follow directly from the so-called \textit{bridge equations} of \cite{e81}, and that is one way to derive them
nodes.statement_short: The alien derivative moves one node forward or arbitrarily many nodes backward, with coefficient $S_k (n+k)$.

nodes.name: Forward Borel residues in terms of $S_1$
nodes.section: 2.4 First Steps Towards Nonlinear Resurgent Analysis
nodes.statement: to which corresponds the closed-form expression\footnote{While this expression could be rewritten using a binomial coefficient, the present form is more natural in light of the upcoming vectorial generalization for multi-parameter transseries (to be discussed in section~\ref{sec:physics}).}: \be \mathsf{S}_{n\to n+k} = - \frac{1}{k!}\, \frac{\left(n+k\right)!}{n!}\, S_1^k. \ee

nodes.name: Backward Borel residues in terms of Stokes constants
nodes.section: 2.4 First Steps Towards Nonlinear Resurgent Analysis
nodes.statement: to which corresponds the closed-form expression\footnote{This expression could be rewritten using sums over partitions (many closed-form formulae of this type may be found in \cite{asv11, as13}). However, in light of the upcoming vectorial generalization for multi-parameter transseries (to be discussed in section~\ref{sec:physics}), it is more natural not to embark in such discussion at this stage.} \be \mathsf{S}_{n\to n-k} = - \sum_{s=1}^{k} \frac{1}{s!}\, \sum_{\substack{\left\{ \ell_1,\ldots,\ell_s\ge 1 \right\} \\ \vphantom{\frac{1}{2}} \sum \ell_i=k}}\, \prod_{a=1}^{s} \left( n - \sum_{j=1}^{a} \ell_j \right)\, \prod_{b=1}^{s} S_{-\ell_b}, \qquad 1\le k < n. \ee

nodes.name: Consistency condition on the Borel residues
nodes.section: 2.4 First Steps Towards Nonlinear Resurgent Analysis
nodes.statement: implies that the Borel residues must satisfy the following consistency condition: \be \mathsf{S}_{n\to n+k} = \frac{(-1)^{k-1}}{k!}\, \prod_{\ell=0}^{k-1} \mathsf{S}_{n+\ell\to n+\ell+1}. \ee

nodes.name: Step $\mathcal{S}$ on the alien chain
nodes.section: 2.4 First Steps Towards Nonlinear Resurgent Analysis
nodes.statement: \item \textit{Step $\mathcal{S}$}: any single link connecting two nodes on the chain

nodes.name: Weight of a step
nodes.section: 2.4 First Steps Towards Nonlinear Resurgent Analysis
nodes.statement: \item \textit{Weight of a step $\mathcal{S}$, $w (\mathcal{S})$}: the product of Stokes coefficient and numerical factor associated with the step, which can be read directly from \eqref{Delta-kA-one-param}. In figure~\ref{fig:first-5-sector-alien-1-param} the weights of the steps are written right next to the colored arrows. For a step connecting nodes $\Phi_m$ and $\Phi_k$ \be w \left( \mathcal{S} \left( m \rightarrow k \right) \right) = k\, S_{k-m}. \ee

nodes.name: Path $\mathcal{P}$ on the alien chain
nodes.section: 2.4 First Steps Towards Nonlinear Resurgent Analysis
nodes.statement: \item \textit{Path $\mathcal{P}$}: a trajectory composed by any number of steps, connecting two nodes $\Phi_m$ to $\Phi_k$ \be \mathcal{P} = \mathcal{S}_1 \cup \mathcal{S}_2 \cup \cdots \cup \mathcal{S}_{\ell}

nodes.name: Length of a path
nodes.section: 2.4 First Steps Towards Nonlinear Resurgent Analysis
nodes.statement: \item \textit{Length of a path $\mathcal{P}$, $\ell (\mathcal{P})$}: the number of steps composing the path (where any step is always considered to have length one) \be \ell (\mathcal{P}) = \# \left\{ \mathcal{S}_i \in \mathcal{P} \right\}. \ee

nodes.name: Weight of a path
nodes.section: 2.4 First Steps Towards Nonlinear Resurgent Analysis
nodes.statement: \item \textit{Weight of a path $\mathcal{P}$, $w (\mathcal{P})$}: the product of the weights of every step composing the path \be w (\mathcal{P}) = \prod_{i=1}^{\ell (\CP)} \,w (\mathcal{S}_i). \ee

nodes.name: Combinatorial factor of a path
nodes.section: 2.4 First Steps Towards Nonlinear Resurgent Analysis
nodes.statement: \item \textit{Combinatorial factor of path $\CP$, $\mathrm{CF} (\mathcal{P})$}: the division by the permutations of $\left\{\mathcal{S}_i\in\mathcal{P}\right\}$ \be \mathrm{CF} (\mathcal{P}) = \frac{1}{\left(\ell (\mathcal{P})\right)!}. \ee

nodes.name: Stokes automorphism on the positive real line acting on $\Phi_2$
nodes.section: 2.4 First Steps Towards Nonlinear Resurgent Analysis
nodes.statement_short: Expanding $\underline{\mathfrak{S}}_0$ on $\Phi_2$ reproduces the single forward paths $\Phi_2\to\Phi_{3,4,5}$ with weights $3S_1$, $12S_1^2$, $60S_1^3$.

nodes.name: Stokes automorphism on the negative real line acting on $\Phi_4$
nodes.section: 2.4 First Steps Towards Nonlinear Resurgent Analysis
nodes.statement_short: Backward motions out of $\Phi_4$ involve several competing paths, whose weights and combinatorial factors reproduce the Borel residues.

nodes.name: Stokes discontinuities from motions on the alien chain
nodes.section: 2.4 First Steps Towards Nonlinear Resurgent Analysis
nodes.statement: \textbf{Stokes discontinuity on positive real line:} $\disc_{0}\Phi_n$ is given by a \textit{sum} over \textit{all} forward paths, linking nodes to the right $\Phi_{m>n}$. \vspace{5pt} \textbf{Stokes discontinuity on negative real line:} $\disc_{\pi}\Phi_n$ is given by a \textit{sum} over \textit{all} backward paths, linking nodes to the left $\Phi_{m<n}$. \vspace{5pt} In both cases each term in this sum ($\Phi_n\rightarrow\Phi_m$) can be decomposed into two factors: \begin{itemize} \item Functional component, dictated solely by beginning and end nodes: \begin{equation*} -\rme^{-\left(m-n\right) \frac{A}{x}}\, \Phi_m. \end{equation*} \item Statistical component, sum over all the allowed paths $\mathcal{P}(n \rightarrow m)$ linking the nodes as in figure~\ref{fig:first-5-sector-alien-1-param}: \begin{equation*} \mathrm{SF}_{(n \rightarrow m)} \equiv \sum_{\mathcal{P}(n \rightarrow m)} \mathrm{CF} (\CP)\, w (\mathcal{P}).
nodes.statement_short: Compute $\disc_\theta \Phi_n$ as a sum over all alien-chain paths, each contributing a functional factor times a statistical factor.
input: $\disc_{0}\Phi_n$ is given by a \textit{sum} over \textit{all} forward paths, linking nodes to the right $\Phi_{m>n}$
$\disc_{\pi}\Phi_n$ is given by a \textit{sum} over \textit{all} backward paths, linking nodes to the left $\Phi_{m<n}$
output: Functional component, dictated solely by beginning and end nodes: \begin{equation*} -\rme^{-\left(m-n\right) \frac{A}{x}}\, \Phi_m. \end{equation*}
Statistical component, sum over all the allowed paths $\mathcal{P}(n \rightarrow m)$ linking the nodes

nodes.name: Forward paths give the discontinuity at $\theta=0$
nodes.section: 2.4 First Steps Towards Nonlinear Resurgent Analysis
nodes.statement: \textbf{Stokes discontinuity on positive real line:} $\disc_{0}\Phi_n$ is given by a \textit{sum} over \textit{all} forward paths, linking nodes to the right $\Phi_{m>n}$.
nodes.statement_short: Along $\theta=0$ sum over all forward paths to nodes on the right.

nodes.name: Backward paths give the discontinuity at $\theta=\pi$
nodes.section: 2.4 First Steps Towards Nonlinear Resurgent Analysis
nodes.statement: \textbf{Stokes discontinuity on negative real line:} $\disc_{\pi}\Phi_n$ is given by a \textit{sum} over \textit{all} backward paths, linking nodes to the left $\Phi_{m<n}$.
nodes.statement_short: Along $\theta=\pi$ sum over all backward paths to nodes on the left.

nodes.name: Functional component of each term
nodes.section: 2.4 First Steps Towards Nonlinear Resurgent Analysis
nodes.statement: \item Functional component, dictated solely by beginning and end nodes: \begin{equation*} -\rme^{-\left(m-n\right) \frac{A}{x}}\, \Phi_m. \end{equation*}
nodes.statement_short: Attach the exponential $-\rme^{-(m-n)A/x}\Phi_m$ fixed by the departure and arrival nodes.

nodes.name: Statistical component of each term
nodes.section: 2.4 First Steps Towards Nonlinear Resurgent Analysis
nodes.statement: \item Statistical component, sum over all the allowed paths $\mathcal{P}(n \rightarrow m)$ linking the nodes as in figure~\ref{fig:first-5-sector-alien-1-param}: \begin{equation*} \mathrm{SF}_{(n \rightarrow m)} \equiv \sum_{\mathcal{P}(n \rightarrow m)} \mathrm{CF} (\CP)\, w (\mathcal{P}).
nodes.statement_short: Multiply by $\mathrm{SF}_{(n\to m)}$, the sum over paths of combinatorial factor times path weight.

nodes.name: Two-parameter transseries for the quartic free energy
nodes.section: 2.4 First Steps Towards Nonlinear Resurgent Analysis
nodes.statement: the \textit{two}-parameter transseries that fully describes the quartic free energy should be \be F (x, \sigma_1, \sigma_2) = \sum_{n=0}^{+\infty} \sum_{m=0}^{+\infty} \sigma_1^n\, \sigma_2^m\, \rme^{-\frac{n A}{x}}\, \Phi_{(n,m)} (x). \ee

nodes.name: ``One-and-a-half'' transseries
nodes.section: 2.4 First Steps Towards Nonlinear Resurgent Analysis
nodes.statement: To reiterate, this is only possible within our example as one of the instanton actions \textit{identically vanishes}; we shall loosely refer to this as having a ``one-and-a-half'' transseries.
nodes.statement_short: A two-parameter transseries with one vanishing instanton action, reorganizable as a one-parameter transseries plus one constant sector.

nodes.name: The ``1.5''-parameter transseries for the quartic free energy
nodes.section: 2.4 First Steps Towards Nonlinear Resurgent Analysis
nodes.statement: let us finally rewrite the transseries solution as \be F (x, \sigma_1, \sigma_2) = \sum_{n=0}^{+\infty} \sigma_1^n\, \rme^{-\frac{n A}{x}}\, \Phi_{(n,0)} (x) + \sigma_2\, F_0^{(0,1)}. \ee

nodes.name: Resurgence relations for the ``1.5''-parameter transseries
nodes.section: 2.4 First Steps Towards Nonlinear Resurgent Analysis
nodes.statement: The resurgence relations which follow from this resurgent singularity-structure are simply \be \Delta_{k A} \Phi_{(n,0)} = S_k \left(n+k\right) \Phi_{(n+k,0)} + \delta_{n+k}\, \widetilde{S}_{-n}\, \Phi_{(0,1)}, \qquad k \le 1 \text{ and } k \neq 0, \ee
nodes.statement_short: The alien derivative can also land on the extra non-asymptotic sector $\Phi_{(0,1)}$, with ``sideways'' Stokes constants $\widetilde{S}_{-n}$.

nodes.name: Stokes constants of the quartic free energy
nodes.section: 2.5 Stokes Constants of Partition Function versus Free Energy
nodes.statement: At the end of the day, one finally obtains \begin{align} S_{-1}^{F} &= - S_{-1}^{Z} &(\, &= - 1\,\, ), \\ \widetilde{S}_{-1}^{F} &= S_{-1}^{Z} &(\, &= 1\,\, ), \\ S_{-m}^{F} &= 0, &&m\ge2, \\ \widetilde{S}_{-m}^{F} &= 0, &&m\ge2. \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: Almost all backward Stokes constants of the free energy vanish: only $S_{-1}^F=-S_{-1}^Z$ and $\widetilde{S}_{-1}^F=S_{-1}^Z$ survive.
assumptions: the resurgence relations for the partition function, \eqref{Delta+A} and \eqref{Delta-A}, alongside the fact that $\Delta_\omega$ is a derivation

nodes.name: Proof that $S_{-k}^{F}=0$ for $k>1$
nodes.section: 2.5 Stokes Constants of Partition Function versus Free Energy
nodes.statement_short: Expand the matching condition order by order in $\tau_1$ and induct: each new order forces $S_{-\ell}^F=0$.

nodes.name: Expand the matching condition for $n=1$
nodes.section: 2.5 Stokes Constants of Partition Function versus Free Energy
nodes.statement: For $n=1$, a power-series expansion of the left-hand side, together with the recursive action of the differential operator on the right-hand side, leads to \begin{eqnarray} \sum_{\ell=0}^{+\infty} \left(-S_{-1}^{Z}\right)^{\ell} \tau_{1}^{\ell+1} & = & \tau_{1} + \sum_{k_{1}=1}^{+\infty} S_{-k_{1}}^{F}\, \tau_{1}^{k_{1}+1} + \frac{1}{2!} \sum_{k_{1},k_{2}=1}^{+\infty} \left( k_{1}+1 \right) S_{-k_{1}}^{F} S_{-k_{2}}^{F}\, \tau_{1}^{k_{1}+k_{2}+1} + \\ &+& \frac{1}{3!} \sum_{k_{1},k_{2},k_{3}=1}^{+\infty} \left( k_{1}+1 \right) \left( k_{1}+k_{2}+1 \right) S_{-k_{1}}^{F} S_{-k_{2}}^{F} S_{-k_{3}}^{F}\, \tau_{1}^{\sum_{i=1}^{3}k_{i}+1} + \cdots. \nonumber \end{eqnarray}
nodes.statement_short: Write both sides of the constraint as power series in $\tau_1$.

nodes.name: Compare equal powers of $\tau_1$
nodes.section: 2.5 Stokes Constants of Partition Function versus Free Energy
nodes.statement: Let us compare equal powers of $\tau_1^{\ell+1}$. For $\ell=0$ we get an identity; for the next few $\ell$'s we find \begin{eqnarray} \ell = 1: & -S_{-1}^{Z} & = S_{-1}^{F}, \\ \ell = 2: & \left( -S_{-1}^{Z} \right)^{2} & = S_{-2}^{F} + \frac{1}{2!} \left( 1+1 \right) \left( S_{-1}^{F} \right)^{2}, \\ \ell = 3: & \left( -S_{-1}^{Z} \right)^{3} & = S_{-3}^{F} + \frac{1}{2!} \left( 2+3 \right) S_{-1}^{F} S_{-2}^{F} + \frac{1}{3!} \left( 2 \times 3 \right) \left( S_{-1}^{F} \right)^{3}. \end{eqnarray}
nodes.statement_short: Match order by order in $\tau_1^{\ell+1}$ for $\ell=1,2,3$.

nodes.name: Solve the first few orders recursively
nodes.section: 2.5 Stokes Constants of Partition Function versus Free Energy
nodes.statement: The first equation above, \eqref{Stokes-comp-one}, immediately yields $S_{-1}^{F} = -S_{-1}^{Z}$. Recursively solving the following equations one sees that \eqref{Stokes-comp-two} then yields $S_{-2}^{F} =0$ and \eqref{Stokes-comp-three} $S_{-3}^{F} =0$. This is a pattern which generalizes to higher powers of $\tau_1$.
nodes.statement_short: Order by order one gets $S_{-1}^F=-S_{-1}^Z$ and then $S_{-2}^F=S_{-3}^F=0$.

nodes.name: Conclude by induction on $\ell$
nodes.section: 2.5 Stokes Constants of Partition Function versus Free Energy
nodes.statement: For a general $\ell$ this looks like \begin{equation} \left( -S_{-1}^{Z} \right)^{\ell} = S_{-\ell}^{F} + \cdots + \frac{1}{\ell!}\, \ell!\left( S_{-1}^{F} \right)^{\ell}, \end{equation} \noindent where the dots indicate terms involving Stokes constants $S_{-k}^F$, $1<k<\ell$, which were already set to zero from previous conditions. By induction, it follows that $S_{-k}^F=0$, for all $k>1$.
nodes.statement_short: At order $\ell$ only $S_{-\ell}^F$ and $(S_{-1}^F)^\ell$ survive, so induction gives $S_{-k}^F=0$ for $k>1$.

nodes.name: Derivation-property argument for the vanishing free-energy Stokes constants
nodes.section: 2.5 Stokes Constants of Partition Function versus Free Energy
nodes.statement: There is yet another way to see how all this is not a big surprise, but rather a straightforward consequence\footnote{In all rigour, this is more of a consistency check that $\Delta_\omega$ is a derivation, as we have not addressed such proof.} of the fact that $\Delta_\omega$ is a derivation. If $\Delta_\omega$ is a derivation and at some specific point $\omega$ one has $\Delta_\omega Z = 0$, then it must be the case that at this same point one finds $\Delta_\omega F = 0$, as $F = \log Z$. But then all the possibilities encoded in \eqref{Delta-kAF:generic} must immediately simplify, as $\Delta_{-kA} Z = 0$ for $k\ge2$. In fact, this condition sets $\Delta_{-kA} F = 0$ for $k\ge2$, which further yields $S_{-k}^{F} = 0$ and $\widetilde{S}_{-k}^{F} = 0$ for $k\ge2$ (indeed, as was later found in \eqref{eq:Stokes-consts-relation-4} and \eqref{eq:Stokes-consts-relation-5}). In other words, the resurgence relations for the partition function, \eqref{Delta+A} and \eqref{Delta-A}, alongside the fact that $\Delta_\omega$ is a derivation, are enough to tell us that the only non-zero result in \eqref{Delta-kAF:generic} must be \be \rme^{\frac{A}{x}} \Delta_{-A} F = \left( S_{-1}^{F}\, \tau_1^{2} \frac{\partial}{\partial\tau_1} + \widetilde{S}_{-1}^F\, \tau_1 \frac{\partial}{\partial\tau_2} \right) F. \ee \noindent But this is precisely what we just had in \eqref{eq:Stokes-aut-pi-v3} above, as expected.
nodes.statement_short: Since $\Delta_\omega$ is a derivation and $F=\log Z$, every vanishing $\Delta_\omega Z$ forces the corresponding $\Delta_\omega F$, hence $S^F_{-k}$, to vanish.

nodes.name: Use that the alien derivative is a derivation
nodes.section: 2.5 Stokes Constants of Partition Function versus Free Energy
nodes.statement: If $\Delta_\omega$ is a derivation and at some specific point $\omega$ one has $\Delta_\omega Z = 0$, then it must be the case that at this same point one finds $\Delta_\omega F = 0$, as $F = \log Z$.
nodes.statement_short: $\Delta_\omega Z = 0$ implies $\Delta_\omega F = 0$ because $F=\log Z$.

nodes.name: Apply it to $\Delta_{-kA} Z = 0$ for $k\ge2$
nodes.section: 2.5 Stokes Constants of Partition Function versus Free Energy
nodes.statement: But then all the possibilities encoded in \eqref{Delta-kAF:generic} must immediately simplify, as $\Delta_{-kA} Z = 0$ for $k\ge2$.
nodes.statement_short: The linear problem has no backward singularities beyond $k=1$.

nodes.name: Conclude the vanishing of $S^F_{-k}$ and $\widetilde{S}^F_{-k}$
nodes.section: 2.5 Stokes Constants of Partition Function versus Free Energy
nodes.statement: In fact, this condition sets $\Delta_{-kA} F = 0$ for $k\ge2$, which further yields $S_{-k}^{F} = 0$ and $\widetilde{S}_{-k}^{F} = 0$ for $k\ge2$
nodes.statement_short: Hence $S_{-k}^F=\widetilde{S}_{-k}^F=0$ for $k\ge2$.

nodes.name: Large-order relations from motions on the alien chain
nodes.section: 2.6 Asymptotics and Large-Order Behaviour: Free Energy
nodes.statement: \textbf{Large-order relations:} The large-order (large $k$) behaviour of the coefficients $F_k^{(n,0)}$, associated to the node $\Phi_{(n,0)}$, is given by a \textit{sum} over \textit{all} forward \textit{and} backward paths, linking nodes to the right $\Phi_{(m>n,0)}$ and to the left $\Phi_{(m<n,0)}$, \textit{in addition} to a sum over paths to the extra ``orthogonal'' node in the chain, $\Phi_{(0,1)}$. \vspace{10pt} Each term in this sum ($\Phi_{(n,0)} \rightarrow \Phi_{(m,\ell=0,1)}$) can be decomposed into three factors: \begin{itemize} \item Leading growth-factor, dictated solely by the order $k$ of the coefficient: \begin{equation*} \frac{\Gamma(k)}{2\pi\rmi\, A^k}. \end{equation*} \noindent \item Large-order factor \eqref{large-order-factor}, dictated by beginning and end nodes: \begin{equation*} \chi_{(n\rightarrow m)}(k). \end{equation*} \noindent \item Statistical factor, sum over all the allowed paths $\mathcal{P}(n \rightarrow m)$ linking the nodes as in figure~\ref{fig:first-5-sector-alien-one-point-five}: \begin{equation*} \mathrm{SF}_{(n \rightarrow m)} \equiv \sum_{\mathcal{P}(n \rightarrow m)} \mathrm{CF} (\CP)\, w (\mathcal{P}).
nodes.statement_short: The large-order growth of $F_k^{(n,0)}$ is a sum over all alien-chain paths of leading growth factor times large-order factor times statistical factor.
input: The large-order (large $k$) behaviour of the coefficients $F_k^{(n,0)}$, associated to the node $\Phi_{(n,0)}$
output: Leading growth-factor, dictated solely by the order $k$ of the coefficient
Large-order factor \eqref{large-order-factor}, dictated by beginning and end nodes
Statistical factor, sum over all the allowed paths $\mathcal{P}(n \rightarrow m)$ linking the nodes

nodes.name: Factor out the leading growth
nodes.section: 2.6 Asymptotics and Large-Order Behaviour: Free Energy
nodes.statement: \item Leading growth-factor, dictated solely by the order $k$ of the coefficient: \begin{equation*} \frac{\Gamma(k)}{2\pi\rmi\, A^k}. \end{equation*}
nodes.statement_short: Divide out $\Gamma(k)/(2\pi\rmi A^k)$.

nodes.name: Attach the large-order factor of each path
nodes.section: 2.6 Asymptotics and Large-Order Behaviour: Free Energy
nodes.statement: \item Large-order factor \eqref{large-order-factor}, dictated by beginning and end nodes: \begin{equation*} \chi_{(n\rightarrow m)}(k). \end{equation*}
nodes.statement_short: Insert $\chi_{(n\to m)}(k)$, determined by departure and arrival nodes.

nodes.name: Weight by the statistical factor and sum
nodes.section: 2.6 Asymptotics and Large-Order Behaviour: Free Energy
nodes.statement: \item Statistical factor, sum over all the allowed paths $\mathcal{P}(n \rightarrow m)$ linking the nodes as in figure~\ref{fig:first-5-sector-alien-one-point-five}: \begin{equation*} \mathrm{SF}_{(n \rightarrow m)} \equiv \sum_{\mathcal{P}(n \rightarrow m)} \mathrm{CF} (\CP)\, w (\mathcal{P}).
nodes.statement_short: Multiply by $\mathrm{SF}_{(n\to m)}$ and sum over arrival nodes.

nodes.name: Large-order factor $\chi_{(n\to m)}$
nodes.section: 2.6 Asymptotics and Large-Order Behaviour: Free Energy
nodes.statement: which we shall denote as the \textit{large-order factor} (the ``statistical component'' will be essentially the same). For a path on the chain, connecting the nodes $\Phi_{(n,0)}\rightarrow \Phi_{(m,c_m)}$, this is \be \chi_{(n\rightarrow m)} (k) \equiv \frac{1}{(m-n)^k}\, \sum_{h=0}^{+\infty} \frac{\Gamma(k-h)}{\Gamma(k)}\, F_h^{(m,c_m)} \left( \left(m-n\right) A\right)^h, \qquad c_m = \left\{ \begin{array}{l} 1, \quad m=0 \\ 0, \quad m>0 \end{array} \right. . \ee

nodes.name: General large-order relation on the alien chain
nodes.section: 2.6 Asymptotics and Large-Order Behaviour: Free Energy
nodes.statement: \noindent Spelled out in writing, the result is: \be F_k^{(n,0)}\, \frac{2\pi\rmi\, A^k}{\Gamma(k)} \simeq \sum_{m\ne n} \mathrm{SF}_{(n\rightarrow m)}\, \chi_{(n\rightarrow m)}(k). \ee

nodes.name: Large-order relation for the perturbative free-energy sector
nodes.section: 2.6 Asymptotics and Large-Order Behaviour: Free Energy
nodes.statement: one may compare equal powers of $x$ on both sides to obtain (after a slight rearrangement)\footnote{In here Stokes coefficients and Borel residues are essentially the same, up to a trivial transformation \eqref{stokesS-to-borelS+GEN}.} \begin{eqnarray} F_{k}^{(0,0)}\, \frac{2\pi\rmi A^k}{\Gamma(k)} &\simeq& S_1 \left( F_0^{(1,0)} + \frac{A}{k-1}\, F_1^{(1,0)} + \frac{A^2}{(k-1)(k-2)}\, F_2^{(1,0)} + \cdots \right) + \\ && + 2^{-k}\, S_1^2 \left( F_0^{(2,0)} + \frac{2A}{k-1}\, F_1^{(2,0)} + \frac{(2A)^2}{(k-1)(k-2)}\, F_2^{(2,0)} + \cdots \right) + \mathcal{O}(3^{-k}). \nonumber \end{eqnarray}
nodes.statement_short: Power-law $1/k$ corrections encode multi-loop data; exponentially suppressed $n^{-k}$ terms encode higher instanton sectors.

nodes.name: Richardson transforms
nodes.section: 2.6 Asymptotics and Large-Order Behaviour: Free Energy
nodes.statement: Richardson extrapolation starts with a $k$-sequence \be \BS (k) \simeq s_0 + \frac{s_1}{k} + \frac{s_2}{k^2} + \cdots, \ee \noindent from where its $N^{\text{th}}$-Richardson transform, herein denoted by $\mathrm{RT}_{\BS} (0,k,N)$, is a new $k$-sequence which can be recursively defined as\footnote{A closed form expression for the $N^{\text{th}}$-Richardson transform is \be \mathrm{RT}_{\BS} (0,k,N) = \sum_{n=0}^N (-1)^{n+N}\, \frac{\left(k+n\right)^N}{n! \left(N-n\right)!}\, \BS(k+n). \ee } \begin{eqnarray} \mathrm{RT}_{\BS} (0,k,0) &=& \BS(k), \\ \mathrm{RT}_{\BS} (0,k,N) &=& \mathrm{RT}_{\BS} (0,k+1,N-1) + \frac{k}{N}\, \Big(\, \mathrm{RT}_{\BS} (0,k+1,N-1) - \mathrm{RT}_{\BS} (0,k,N-1)\, \Big), \\ && \hspace{+340pt} N \ge 1. \nonumber \end{eqnarray}
nodes.statement_short: Recursively cancel the subleading $1/k$ corrections of a sequence so as to converge fast onto its leading term $s_0$.
output: a new $k$-sequence which can be recursively defined as

nodes.name: Initialize the zeroth Richardson transform
nodes.section: 2.6 Asymptotics and Large-Order Behaviour: Free Energy
nodes.statement: \mathrm{RT}_{\BS} (0,k,0) &=& \BS(k)
nodes.statement_short: Start from the sequence itself.

nodes.name: Iterate the Richardson recursion
nodes.section: 2.6 Asymptotics and Large-Order Behaviour: Free Energy
nodes.statement: \mathrm{RT}_{\BS} (0,k,N) &=& \mathrm{RT}_{\BS} (0,k+1,N-1) + \frac{k}{N}\, \Big(\, \mathrm{RT}_{\BS} (0,k+1,N-1) - \mathrm{RT}_{\BS} (0,k,N-1)\, \Big)
nodes.statement_short: Each iteration removes one more power of $1/k$.

nodes.name: Borel--Pad\'e resummation
nodes.section: 2.6 Asymptotics and Large-Order Behaviour: Free Energy
nodes.statement:
given an asymptotic series $\BS(k)$, with zero radius of convergence, its Borel transform  e \CB [\BS] (t) = \sum_{m=0}^{+\infty}  rac{s_m}{\Gamma(m+1)}\, t^m \ee 
oindent will instead have a (finite) non-zero radius of convergence. Of course as long as there are no closed-form expressions for all the coefficients $s_m$, one cannot precisely pinpoint the above analytic function. However, using the recursion relations for, 	extit{e.g.}, the free energy coefficients listed in the appendix, we have computationally calculated them in our example up to $2N=120$. If we make sole use of these resulting coefficients, what we have managed to compute is  e \CB [\BS] (t) \approx \sum_{m=0}^{2N}  rac{s_m}{\Gamma(m+1)}\, t^m. \ee 
oindent Now instead of immediately ``inverting'' this result via Borel resummation \eqref{borelresum} (which at this point would only allow us to recover these first $2N$ terms of the asymptotic expansion $\BS(k)$), we shall first approximate the above 	extit{truncated} Borel transform by an order-$N$ diagonal Pad'e approximant, as in:  e \mathrm{BP}_N [\BS] (t) =  rac{\sum_{\ell=0}^{N} a_n\, t^n}{\sum_{\ell=0}^{N} b_n\, t^n}, \ee 
oindent where the coefficients $a_n$, $b_n$ are chosen to match the ones in the expansion of the Borel transform in a small-$t$ expansion. The main reason for choosing this rational function instead of the expansion \eqref{borel-S} is that, while for small $t$ they are basically the same, for large $t$ the rational function converges to a constant and is much better behaved ootnote{When performing Borel resummation \eqref{borelresum}, we need to integrate over the range of both $t$ small 	extit{and} large!}. Moreover, the poles of this rational function will also prove to be very good approximations (upon ``condensation'') to the branch-cuts of the Borel transform. It is then to the rational function \eqref{pade-S} which we apply Borel resumation, along the positive real axis (as the original variable $k$ is the order of the coefficients, and is thus positive),  e \CS_0 \mathrm{BP}_{N} [\BS] (k) = \int_0^{+\infty} md t\, \mathrm{BP}_N [\BS] \left(  rac{t}{k} ight) me^{-t}. \ee 
oindent As should be familiar by now, this integration can only be performed when there are no poles of $\mathrm{BP}_N [\BS] (t)$ along the positive real axis of the Borel $t$-plane. However, this is very many times the case, and in such situations one needs to shift the integration contour off the real axis, say by performing a lateral Borel resummation, 	extit{e.g.}, $\CS_{0^{-}} \mathrm{BP}_{N} [\BS] (k)$.
nodes.statement_short: Truncate the Borel transform, replace it by a diagonal Pad\'e approximant, and Laplace-transform back, shifting the contour laterally if poles sit on the axis.
input: an asymptotic series $\BS(k)$, with zero radius of convergence

nodes.name: Truncate the Borel transform at order $2N$
nodes.section: 2.6 Asymptotics and Large-Order Behaviour: Free Energy
nodes.statement: If we make sole use of these resulting coefficients, what we have managed to compute is \be \CB [\BS] (t) \approx \sum_{m=0}^{2N} \frac{s_m}{\Gamma(m+1)}\, t^m. \ee
nodes.statement_short: Use the recursively computed coefficients up to $2N$.

nodes.name: Build the diagonal Pad\'e approximant
nodes.section: 2.6 Asymptotics and Large-Order Behaviour: Free Energy
nodes.statement: we shall first approximate the above \textit{truncated} Borel transform by an order-$N$ diagonal Pad\'e approximant, as in: \be \mathrm{BP}_N [\BS] (t) = \frac{\sum_{\ell=0}^{N} a_n\, t^n}{\sum_{\ell=0}^{N} b_n\, t^n}, \ee \noindent where the coefficients $a_n$, $b_n$ are chosen to match the ones in the expansion of the Borel transform in a small-$t$ expansion.
nodes.statement_short: Replace the truncated series by a rational function whose poles condense onto the Borel branch cuts.

nodes.name: Borel resum the rational approximant
nodes.section: 2.6 Asymptotics and Large-Order Behaviour: Free Energy
nodes.statement: It is then to the rational function \eqref{pade-S} which we apply Borel resumation, along the positive real axis (as the original variable $k$ is the order of the coefficients, and is thus positive), \be \CS_0 \mathrm{BP}_{N} [\BS] (k) = \int_0^{+\infty} \rmd t\, \mathrm{BP}_N [\BS] \left( \frac{t}{k} \right) \rme^{-t}. \ee
nodes.statement_short: Laplace-transform the Pad\'e approximant along the positive real axis.

nodes.name: Shift the contour laterally when poles sit on the axis
nodes.section: 2.6 Asymptotics and Large-Order Behaviour: Free Energy
nodes.statement: However, this is very many times the case, and in such situations one needs to shift the integration contour off the real axis, say by performing a lateral Borel resummation, \textit{e.g.}, $\CS_{0^{-}} \mathrm{BP}_{N} [\BS] (k)$.
nodes.statement_short: Use a lateral resummation, producing real and imaginary parts that must be treated separately.

nodes.name: Iterative construction of a transseries solution in harder problems
nodes.section: 2.6 Asymptotics and Large-Order Behaviour: Free Energy
nodes.statement: In general, in harder problems (and without a linear ``companion-problem'' to help us bypass some of the nonlinear difficulties), the procedure develops in the opposite direction, or as a mix in-between. One puts forward a reasonable \textit{ansatz} for a transseries solution, then checks it via large-order relations as above. Some aspects may be validated, others not---and require for extra structure to be added to the transseries \textit{ansatz}. So one does, and repeats the different analyses and checks. Iteratively, one eventually constructs the full resurgent transseries solution to the problem at hand (also sometimes involving numerical determination of many Stokes constants).
nodes.statement_short: Propose a transseries ansatz, test it against large-order relations, enlarge it where the tests fail, and iterate.

nodes.name: $d$-dimensional partition function
nodes.section: 3 Lefschetz Thimbles for Linear Problems
nodes.statement: Let us begin with a $d$-dimensional ``partition function'', given by the integral \be Z (\hbar) = \frac{1}{\left( 2\pi \right)^d} \int_{\boldsymbol{\Gamma}} \rmd z^1 \wedge \cdots \wedge \rmd z^d\, \rme^{- \frac{1}{\hbar} V(\boldsymbol{z})}. \ee

nodes.name: Isolated non-degenerate critical points
nodes.section: 3 Lefschetz Thimbles for Linear Problems
nodes.statement: We shall further assume that the critical points of the potential, $V$, are isolated and non-degenerate, \textit{i.e.}, the determinant of the Hessian matrix of $V$, $\text{Hess} \equiv \det (\partial_a\partial_b V)$, at these critical points is non-zero.

nodes.name: Homology classification of convergent integration cycles
nodes.section: 3 Lefschetz Thimbles for Linear Problems
nodes.statement: In fact, the main result we now wish to discuss is that any integration cycle, $\boldsymbol{\Gamma}$, over which \eqref{eq:nd_integral} is convergent, is a $d$-\textit{cycle} with \textit{integer coefficients}. Furthermore, the partition-function integral will subsequently only depend upon the \textit{homology class} of $\boldsymbol{\Gamma}$ in the relative\footnote{A $d$-cycle $\gamma$ in $\mathbb C^d$ is called a \textit{relative cycle} mod $\CX$ if its boundary, $\partial \gamma$, lies in $\CX$ (if we think of $\BC^d$ as a $2d$-dimensional real manifold, then $\CX$ is a $(2d-1)$-dimensional real manifold). A natural equivalence class of relative $d$-cycles is simply constructed by saying that two cycles $\gamma$ and $\gamma'$ are equivalent iff $\gamma-\gamma^{\prime}$ is homologous to zero. Then the relative homology group $H_d (\BC^d, \CX; \BZ )$ is the set of these equivalence classes with integer coefficients.} homology group $H_d ( \BC^d, \CX_\epsilon; \BZ )$ \cite{p83, f77, w10a}. Now, the properties of this relative homology group depend only upon the local properties of the potential, $V$, near its critical points. Moreover, a basis for this homology group may be identified with the equivalence classes of integration cycles which intersect only \textit{one}\footnote{The violation of this requirement concerning critical points leads to Stokes phenomenon, to be discussed later.} critical point, $\boldsymbol{z}^*_i$, and which we shall denote by $\left\{ \CJ_i \right\}$.
nodes.statement_short: Convergent cycles are integral $d$-cycles whose homology class in $H_d(\BC^d,\CX_\epsilon;\BZ)$ is all that the integral sees; the Lefschetz thimbles form a basis.
assumptions: any integration cycle, $\boldsymbol{\Gamma}$, over which \eqref{eq:nd_integral} is convergent
conclusions: the partition-function integral will subsequently only depend upon the \textit{homology class} of $\boldsymbol{\Gamma}$
a basis for this homology group may be identified with the equivalence classes of integration cycles which intersect only \textit{one}

nodes.name: Thimble decomposition of the integration cycle
nodes.section: 3 Lefschetz Thimbles for Linear Problems
nodes.statement: It then turns out that, in this case, the original cycle $\boldsymbol{\Gamma}$ can be decomposed as \be \boldsymbol{\Gamma} = \sum_{i=1}^N n_i\, \CJ_i, \ee \noindent leading to \be \int_{\boldsymbol{\Gamma}} \rmd z^1 \wedge \cdots \wedge \rmd z^d = \sum_{i=1}^N n_i\, \int_{\CJ_i} \rmd z^1 \wedge \cdots \wedge \rmd z^d, \ee \noindent where the $n_i$'s are integers and $N$ is the total number of critical points. The cycles $\CJ_i$ are what is known as the \textit{Lefschetz thimbles}.

nodes.name: Gradient flow equations
nodes.section: 3 Lefschetz Thimbles for Linear Problems
nodes.statement: Moreover, this convergence will be fastest along that collection of curves (parameterized by $\tau$) which flow along the \textit{gradient} of the above function, \textit{i.e.}, along \be \frac{\rmd\boldsymbol{z}}{\rmd\tau} = - 2\, \frac{\partial\rho}{\partial\bar{\boldsymbol{z}}}. \ee \noindent This set of equations \eqref{eq:gradient_flow} is known as the \textit{gradient flow equations}

nodes.name: Proof that the height function decreases along downward flow
nodes.section: 3 Lefschetz Thimbles for Linear Problems
nodes.statement: It is then straightforward to show that $\rho \left( \boldsymbol{z}(\tau) \right)$ \textit{decreases} along any curve with increasing $\tau$: \begin{equation} \frac{\rmd \rho \left( \boldsymbol{z}(\tau) \right)}{\rmd\tau} = \frac{\partial\rho}{\partial\boldsymbol{z}} \cdot \frac{\rmd\boldsymbol{z}}{\rmd\tau} = - 2 \left| \frac{\partial\rho}{\partial\boldsymbol{z}} \right|^2 \leq 0. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Chain rule on the gradient flow gives $\rmd\rho/\rmd\tau = -2|\partial\rho/\partial\boldsymbol{z}|^2 \le 0$.

nodes.name: Lefschetz thimble
nodes.section: 3 Lefschetz Thimbles for Linear Problems
nodes.statement: It is the set of all points that may be reached out from a given critical point, $\boldsymbol{z}^*_i$, via downward flow as above, which is called a \textit{Lefschetz thimble} (associated with the critical point\footnote{Following our assumption that there is only \textit{one} critical point associated with a given thimble---and deferring the discussion of Stokes phenomenon, which occurs when this assumption is violated, to the end of this section.} $\boldsymbol{z}^*_i$). Expanding the potential around the critical point, one can use Morse theory to show that there are $d$ real, orthogonal directions along which one can flow downwards. Therefore, the thimble generated by the collection of all such flows is a $d$-real-dimensional cycle.
nodes.statement_short: The set of points reachable from a critical point by downward gradient flow; a $d$-real-dimensional cycle generalizing the steepest-descent contour.
differentia: the set of all points that may be reached out from a given critical point, $\boldsymbol{z}^*_i$, via downward flow

nodes.name: Vanishing cycle
nodes.section: 3 Lefschetz Thimbles for Linear Problems
nodes.statement: This $(d-1)$-sphere is known as the \textit{vanishing cycle}; vanishing at the critical point (for $d=1$, the vanishing cycle is just two points).

nodes.name: Proof that the imaginary part of the potential is constant on a thimble
nodes.section: 3 Lefschetz Thimbles for Linear Problems
nodes.statement: To see how this comes about, let us split the complex coordinates $\boldsymbol{z}$ into their real and imaginary parts, $\boldsymbol{z} = \boldsymbol{x} + \rmi \boldsymbol{y}$, and use the Cauchy--Riemann equations to obtain \begin{eqnarray} \frac{\rmd\boldsymbol{x}}{\rmd\tau} &=& - \frac{\partial\rho}{\partial\boldsymbol{x}} = - \frac{\partial}{\partial\boldsymbol{y}}\, \im \left( - \frac{1}{\hbar} V (\boldsymbol{z}) \right), \\ \frac{\rmd\boldsymbol{y}}{\rmd\tau} &=& - \frac{\partial\rho}{\partial\boldsymbol{y}} = \frac{\partial}{\partial\boldsymbol{x}}\, \im \left( - \frac{1}{\hbar} V (\boldsymbol{z}) \right), \end{eqnarray} \noindent from where it follows \begin{equation} \frac{\rmd}{\rmd\tau}\, \im \left( - \frac{1}{\hbar} V (\boldsymbol{z}) \right) = \frac{\rmd\boldsymbol{x}}{\rmd\tau} \cdot \frac{\partial}{\partial\boldsymbol{x}}\, \im \left( - \frac{1}{\hbar} V (\boldsymbol{z}) \right) + \frac{\rmd\boldsymbol{y}}{\rmd\tau} \cdot \frac{\partial}{\partial\boldsymbol{y}}\, \im \left( - \frac{1}{\hbar} V (\boldsymbol{z}) \right) = 0. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Split $\boldsymbol{z}=\boldsymbol{x}+\rmi\boldsymbol{y}$ and use Cauchy--Riemann; the $\tau$-derivative of $\im(-V/\hbar)$ cancels identically.

nodes.name: Picard--Lefschetz (complex gradient flow) equation
nodes.section: 3 Lefschetz Thimbles for Linear Problems
nodes.statement: This is the \textit{complex} gradient flow equation, also known as \textit{Picard--Lefschetz equation}, whose solutions then naturally satisfy \eqref{saddlegeneratethimble}.

nodes.name: Intersection pairing of upward and downward thimbles
nodes.section: 3 Lefschetz Thimbles for Linear Problems
nodes.statement: Given two cycles $\boldsymbol{\Gamma}$ and $\boldsymbol{\Gamma}^\prime$, one can define an inner product via the intersection number \be \left\langle\, \CK_n, \CJ_m\, \right\rangle = \delta_{nm}\,. \ee

nodes.name: Distinct imaginary parts of the critical values
nodes.section: 3 Lefschetz Thimbles for Linear Problems
nodes.statement:
To start off with, let us impose a constraint regarding the critical points; which is that no pair of critical values has the same imaginary part, 	extit{i.e.},  e \im \left(  rac{1}{\hbar} V ( oldsymbol{z}^*_i) ight) 
eq \im \left(  rac{1}{\hbar} V ( oldsymbol{z}^*_j) ight) \quad 	ext{for} \quad i
eq j. \ee 
oindent Since the imaginary part is a conserved quantity along the thimble, this assumption guarantees that there are no intersections between thimbles associated with different critical points, and the decomposition of the integration cycle \eqref{eq:decomposition} is thus well defined.

nodes.name: Transseries form of the multi-dimensional partition function
nodes.section: 3 Lefschetz Thimbles for Linear Problems
nodes.statement: Using the decomposition of $\boldsymbol{\Gamma}$ into thimbles \eqref{eq:decomposition}, we find that the partition function in fact has a \textit{transseries} form, as \be Z (\hbar) = \frac{1}{\left( 2\pi \right)^d} \int_{\boldsymbol{\Gamma}} \rme^{- \frac{1}{\hbar} V(\boldsymbol{z})}\, \Omega = \hbar^{\frac{d}{2}}\, \sum_{i=1}^N n_i\, \rme^{- \frac{1}{\hbar} V^*_i} \Phi_i(\hbar), \ee \noindent where each $\Phi_i(\hbar)$ is an asymptotic series \be \Phi_i (\hbar) \simeq \sum_{k=0}^{+\infty} Z^{(i)}_k \hbar^{k} \ee
nodes.statement_short: Each thimble contributes one exponential times an asymptotic series, so $Z$ is a finite transseries indexed by the critical points.
assumptions: the decomposition of $\boldsymbol{\Gamma}$ into thimbles \eqref{eq:decomposition}
conclusions: the partition function in fact has a \textit{transseries} form

nodes.name: Picard--Lefschetz formula
nodes.section: 3 Lefschetz Thimbles for Linear Problems
nodes.statement: which is captured by the \textit{Picard--Lefschetz formula} \cite{l24} \be \CV_n ( \mathsf{r}_{nm}\, \rme^{\rmi \left( \phi + 2\pi \right)} ) = \CV_n ( \mathsf{r}_{nm}\, \rme^{\rmi\phi} ) + \left(-1\right)^{\frac{d \left(d-1\right)}{2}}\, \mathsf{S}_{nm}\, \CV_m ( \mathsf{r}_{nm}\, \rme^{\rmi\phi} ). \ee \noindent Here, $\mathsf{r}_{nm}\, \rme^{\rmi\phi}$ parameterizes an infinitesimal circle around $V^*_{nm}$, and the coefficient $\mathsf{S}_{nm}$ is the intersection number of the two vanishing cycles, $\mathsf{S}_{nm} \equiv \langle \CV_n, \CV_m \rangle \in \BZ$.
nodes.statement_short: Transporting a vanishing cycle around a singularity adds the other vanishing cycle, weighted by their intersection number.

nodes.name: Monodromy of the generalized Borel transform
nodes.section: 3 Lefschetz Thimbles for Linear Problems
nodes.statement: Simply plugging the monodromy \eqref{eq:picard_lefschetz} in \eqref{eq:Borel_van}, one obtains \be \CB_-[\Psi_n](s) = \CB_+[\Psi_n](s) + \left(-1\right)^{\frac{d \left(d-1\right)}{2}}\, \mathsf{S}_{nm}\, \CB_+[\Psi_m](s). \ee

nodes.name: Resurgent relations for thimble sectors in even and odd dimension
nodes.section: 3 Lefschetz Thimbles for Linear Problems
nodes.statement: It is worth mentioning that the resurgent relations take a standard form in this setting \cite{dh02} \begin{eqnarray} \CB[\Psi_n](s) \Big|_{s=V^*_{nm}} &=& \mathsf{S}_{nm}\, \CB[\Psi_m] (s-V^*_{nm})\, \frac{\log (s-V^*_{nm})}{2\pi\rmi} + \text{holomorphic}, \qquad d = \text{even}, \\ \CB[\Psi_n](s) \Big|_{s=V^*_{nm}} &=& - \frac{1}{2}\, \mathsf{S}_{nm}\, \CB[\Psi_m] (s-V^*_{nm}) + \text{holomorphic}, \qquad\qquad\qquad\, d = \text{odd}. \end{eqnarray}

nodes.name: Renormalization obstructs the thimble construction in quantum field theory
nodes.section: 3 Lefschetz Thimbles for Linear Problems
nodes.statement: But this factoring can only be done when considering \textit{bare} quantities. As renormalization kicks in, the coupling runs as $\lambda \equiv \lambda (\mu)$ at energy-scale $\mu$, further inducing mass renormalization and wave-function renormalization. For our purposes, the overall effect of such renormalization procedure is to \textit{invalidate} the above factoring. One rather finds (very schematically---see \cite{k16} for a full discussion) \be S (\varphi) \to \frac{1}{\lambda} S_{-1} (\widetilde{\varphi} ) + S_{0} (\widetilde{\varphi} ) + \lambda S_{1} (\widetilde{\varphi} ) + \lambda^2 S_{2} (\widetilde{\varphi} ) + \cdots. \ee \noindent This automatically implies that in order to address renormalizable quantum field theories, one will need more sophisticated saddle-point methods and answers than just \eqref{eq:thimble_asymp}, and likely more complicated transseries structures than the ones we have been addressing so far
nodes.statement_short: A running coupling spoils the factorization $S\to S/\lambda$, so renormalizable QFTs need richer transseries than the thimble expansion.

nodes.name: Borel transform with a general offset $\beta_n$
nodes.section: 4 Borel Transforms for Nonlinear Problems
nodes.statement: The Borel transform is thus written as \begin{equation} \CB[\Phi_n] (s) = \sum_{k=0}^{+\infty} \left( 1 - \delta_{k,0} \delta_{\beta_{n},0} \right) Z_{k}^{(n)}\, \frac{s^{k+\beta_n-1}}{\Gamma (k+\beta_n)}. \end{equation}

nodes.section: 4 Borel Transforms for Nonlinear Problems
nodes.statement: it can also be written as a contour integral\footnote{Notice that this calculation also helps making \eqref{eq:Borel_van} a bit more explicit.}, \begin{equation} \CB[\Psi_{n}](s) = \frac{1}{2\pi} \left\{ \frac{\widetilde{g} \left( x_{+}(s) \right)}{\frac{\rmd v^{(n)}}{\rmd x} \left( x_{+}(s) \right)} - \frac{\widetilde{g} \left( x_{-}(s) \right)}{\frac{\rmd v^{(n)}}{\rmd x} \left( x_{-}(s) \right)}\right\} = \frac{1}{4\pi^{2}\rmi}\, \frac{1}{\sqrt{s}} \oint_{\Gamma_{\circlearrowleft}} \rmd x\, \frac{\sqrt{v^{(n)} (x)}}{v^{(n)} (x) - s}\, \widetilde{g}(x). \end{equation}
